name: Economic Development & Industry
description: Iran combines a substantial domestic economy with an energy sector whose export earnings influence public finances and investment. Understanding its development requires examining production, infrastructure, employment, trade, and environmental constraints together.

seo.title: Economic Development & Industry in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran's economic structure, energy dependencies, industrial connections, and the evidence needed to assess development.

content.heading: An economy connected through energy
content.content:
Iran's economy extends beyond petroleum, but energy remains an important connection between domestic production and external earnings. The U.S. Energy Information Administration describes a relatively diversified economy in which petroleum exports nevertheless provide significant government revenue. Its assessment also identifies sanctions and underinvestment as constraints on the energy sector. Resource abundance therefore does not establish how much productive capacity is available or how easily export income can finance development. [s1]

Energy also enters the economy through domestic consumption. Natural gas and petroleum supplied almost all primary energy consumption in the EIA's assessment for 2022. That dependence connects the energy system to questions about industrial reliability and investment: the existence of reserves underground is different from the ability to deliver usable energy where it is needed. [s1]

content.heading: Infrastructure and work
content.content:
The World Bank's October 2025 assessment reported that water and energy shortages were disrupting economic activity. It connected water scarcity to drought, climate change, and resource management, and identified land subsidence as a threat to infrastructure and productivity. These are development constraints as well as environmental concerns. A useful industrial assessment must therefore ask about continuity of supply alongside installed capacity. [s2]

The same assessment identified services as the largest employer and described substantial barriers to translating economic activity into broad employment. This complicates a development story focused only on factories or export volumes. Work, access to infrastructure, and the resilience of everyday services belong in the assessment alongside production. The report's findings describe its research period; they do not independently establish conditions throughout 2026. [s2]

content.heading: Reading the branches together
content.content:
The directory's branches provide complementary routes through this subject. Macroeconomics supplies the framework for interpreting aggregate output. Oil and gas concerns a major source of export earnings and domestic energy. Transport, construction, employment, and regional development provide further questions for evaluating how production supports economic life.

The World Bank's Iran Economic Monitor treats macroeconomic developments, financial markets, and human welfare as connected subjects. Its publication archive also documents changing analytical priorities, including job creation, poverty, water security, and the effects of sanctions and the pandemic. That breadth is a useful guide to reading this section: growth needs to be examined alongside its sources, durability, and consequences for people. [s3]

This page is an introductory research draft. The evidence inspected supports the connections discussed here, but a publication-ready national survey still requires direct research into the individual industries and their regional distribution.

name: Macroeconomics
description: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide output, prices, employment, and financial relationships. For Iran, interpreting these measures requires particular care over reporting periods, exchange-rate conventions, and the distinction between historical observations and forecasts.

seo.title: Understanding Iran's Macroeconomy | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: A guide to interpreting Iranian output statistics, reporting calendars, exchange-rate conventions, and economic forecasts.

content.heading: Start with the measurement
content.content:
National accounts organize information about production, income, and expenditure into a consistent framework. Gross domestic product, or GDP, is a central aggregate within that framework. The World Bank's metadata describes production, expenditure, and income as alternative approaches to measuring it. These approaches help distinguish a change in total economic activity from a change in one particular industry. [s1]

Comparability is a practical problem. Services can be difficult to measure, informal activities require estimation, and rebasing can change the weights used in national accounts. A historical series may consequently be revised even when the underlying period is long past. Keeping the dataset code and release context is part of interpreting the number, rather than merely an administrative detail. [s1]

content.heading: Currency conventions change comparisons
content.content:
A dollar-denominated GDP figure depends on a conversion convention. The IMF's May 2023 regional statistical appendix provides a concrete Iranian example: its historical nominal GDP calculations used the official exchange rate through 2017 and the NIMA exchange rate from 2018. The appendix explains that staff considered the latter more representative of transaction values. This is a documented convention for that publication, not a rule that can be assumed for every Iranian dataset. [s2]

Purchasing power parity, or PPP, answers a different question. The World Bank's International Comparison Program compares prices and expenditure to account for differences in purchasing power across economies. Its methodology requires comparable national-account definitions and coverage. A PPP comparison is therefore not interchangeable with converting output at a financial exchange rate. [s3]

content.heading: Keep the release and period attached
content.content:
The World Bank's Spring/Summer 2023 Iran Economic Monitor illustrates why a table must be read with its column labels. Its selected-indicators table separates actual results, estimates, and projections, and reports Iranian years using paired labels such as 2022/23. A projection does not become an observed result simply because its reporting period has subsequently ended. [s4]

The IMF likewise explains that historical WEO estimates are revised as country teams receive updated information from national authorities. Comparisons should therefore identify both the period being measured and the publication supplying the value. Combining historical numbers from different releases without checking revisions can create a series that no institution actually published. [s5]

The next step is to read output alongside prices, employment, productivity, and distribution. The linked pages separate those questions so that a GDP total does not have to stand in for every aspect of economic performance. Those companion indicators still require dedicated Iranian source research before this overview can offer a complete account of their relationships.

name: Gross Domestic Product
description: Gross domestic product measures production within an economy over a reporting period. Iran's nominal GDP in current U.S. dollars is useful as a published monetary series, but changes in it must not be interpreted directly as changes in real output or household welfare.

seo.title: Iran's Gross Domestic Product: Meaning and Annual Data | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Inspect Iran's published nominal GDP series and understand why current-dollar values differ from real economic growth.

content.heading: What GDP counts
content.content:
Gross domestic product measures the value of final goods and services produced within an economy during a period. The production approach adds value created at successive stages, avoiding the repeated counting of intermediate inputs. Income and expenditure approaches examine the same production through the incomes it generates and the final purchases associated with it. [s1]

The distinction between nominal and real GDP is essential. Nominal GDP values production at current prices. Real GDP adjusts for price changes to examine changes in output. Neither measure, on its own, establishes how income is distributed or whether environmental damage has accompanied production. GDP is an important economic aggregate, but it is not a complete measure of well-being. [s1]

content.heading: The annual series presented here
content.content:
The dataset below reproduces World Bank current-dollar GDP observations distributed through the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's FRED service. The inspected series identifies its source as World Development Indicators, its frequency as annual, and its units as current U.S. dollars. Its displayed update predates the editorial cutoff. The requested default window is represented from 2012 through 2026; the unfinished final year is missing. [s2]

The chart shows substantial variation in the dollar valuation of Iranian production. It does not isolate changes in production volumes. No exchange-rate conversion has been performed here, and no growth rate has been calculated from these nominal values. The precision retained reflects the published download, rather than a claim that national output is measured with comparable economic certainty. [s2]

FRED labels annual observations with January dates. Those labels are retained as year identifiers, without treating them as verified boundaries of Iran's underlying national-account periods. Resolving that calendar mapping and documenting the World Bank's Iran-specific currency conversion are necessary before stronger comparative conclusions can be drawn. [s2]

content.title: Iran: published nominal GDP in current U.S. dollars
content.interpretation: The published current-dollar value falls between 2012 and 2015, rises in 2016–2017, falls through 2020, rises through 2024, and falls in 2025. These movements describe nominal dollar valuation, not real output growth. No value is available here for 2026. [s2]

content.title: Published annual GDP observations and the missing final year

content.heading: Choosing a comparison
content.content:
Purchasing-power comparisons address differences in price levels across economies. The World Bank's International Comparison Program uses prices and national-account expenditure information to construct purchasing power parities. Its framework distinguishes consumption, capital formation, and net exports, while emphasizing comparable definitions and coverage. A PPP estimate and a current-dollar GDP total therefore answer different questions. [s3]

For this page, the defensible conclusion is limited: an inspected annual nominal series is available, but it does not establish Iran's real growth path. A fuller account requires a comparable constant-price series, an explicit treatment of reporting calendars, and documentation of revisions. Until those checks are complete, the page remains a research draft.
